description: Slum clearance to COVID-19 — how government shaped public health in twentieth-century Britain.
content_html:
Public Health in the Modern Age

By 1900, the major legislative framework for Victorian public health was in place — the 1875 Public Health Act had established compulsory sanitary standards, and the worst cholera epidemics had ended. But the twentieth century brought new public health challenges: overcrowded and inadequate housing, industrial air pollution, smoking-related disease, obesity, and eventually new viral pandemics. The response involved a shift from reactive legislation to proactive campaigns, combining government action with mass communication.

Housing Reform and Slum Clearance

In the early twentieth century, many British working-class families still lived in the overcrowded and insanitary housing that had been built during the Industrial Revolution. After the First World War, the government committed to a programme of social housing. The 1919 Addison Act required local authorities to build council housing to meet local needs, with central government subsidies. Hundreds of thousands of council houses were built in the interwar period, moving families out of the worst Victorian slums and into houses with gardens, indoor sanitation and proper ventilation. Slum clearance programmes in cities like Liverpool, Glasgow and Birmingham during the 1930s replaced some of the worst housing, though the scale of the problem meant progress was slow.

Key Fact

The 1919 Addison Act launched a programme of council house building, providing working-class families with homes that had indoor sanitation and proper ventilation for the first time. Slum clearance in the 1930s demolished the worst Victorian housing. By 1939, around one million council homes had been built in Britain.

Tackling Air Pollution: The Clean Air Act 1956

Industrial and domestic coal burning created severe air pollution in British towns and cities throughout the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. The problem came to a head with the Great Smog of London in December 1952: a combination of fog and coal smoke created a toxic smog that blanketed the city for five days. Estimates suggest it killed between 4,000 and 12,000 people, mostly through respiratory and cardiovascular disease. The episode provoked public outrage and political pressure for action. The Clean Air Act 1956 introduced smokeless zones in urban areas, banning the burning of coal in domestic fires, and set emission standards for industry. Air quality in British cities improved significantly over the following decades.

Tobacco smoking rose sharply in Britain during and after the First World War. In 1950, epidemiologists Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill published research in the British Medical Journal demonstrating a clear statistical link between smoking and lung cancer. The government’s response was initially cautious, partly because of the tax revenue generated by tobacco. Health warnings were added to cigarette packets from 1971. Television advertising for cigarettes was banned in 1965. Sponsorship of sporting events by tobacco companies was progressively restricted. The most decisive intervention came in 2007, when smoking was banned in all enclosed public places in England under the Health Act 2006. Similar bans had already been introduced in Scotland (2006) and Wales (2007). The smoking ban was accompanied by NHS stop-smoking services and extensive public health campaigns. Smoking rates in Britain fell from around 45 per cent of adults in 1974 to below 15 per cent by the 2020s.

Healthy Eating and Obesity Campaigns

By the late twentieth century, the primary public health challenges in Britain had shifted from infectious diseases to non-communicable conditions — obesity, type 2 diabetes, heart disease and cancer — strongly linked to lifestyle choices. The government launched the Change4Life campaign in 2009, promoting exercise, healthier eating and reducing alcohol consumption, particularly targeting children and families. The “five-a-day” campaign, promoting the consumption of five portions of fruit and vegetables daily, had been introduced in the early 2000s. The government’s sugar tax, introduced in 2018 on soft drinks, was a more interventionist measure, using taxation rather than persuasion to discourage consumption of high-sugar products.

Key Fact

Key twentieth and twenty-first century public health interventions include: Clean Air Act 1956 (air pollution), smoking ban 2007 (tobacco-related disease), Change4Life 2009 (obesity and inactivity), sugar tax 2018 (childhood obesity and diabetes). All demonstrate the shift from Victorian sanitation to lifestyle-focused public health.

The COVID-19 pandemic, which reached Britain in early 2020, tested the entire apparatus of modern public health. The government introduced a national lockdown from March 2020 — the most extensive restriction of daily life in peacetime British history. Social distancing rules, mask mandates, and the closure of hospitality and leisure venues attempted to slow transmission of the virus. The NHS vaccination programme, launched in December 2020 with the Pfizer–BioNTech vaccine, was the most rapid mass vaccination in British history. By mid-2021, the majority of British adults had received at least one dose. The pandemic demonstrated both the capabilities of modern public health (rapid vaccine development, mass vaccination logistics) and the challenges (supply chain difficulties, vaccine hesitancy, disproportionate impact on deprived communities and ethnic minorities). It also drew explicit parallels with past public health crises: quarantine, long used against plague, returned; public health communication campaigns echoed First World War government information drives.
exam_tip_html: When answering questions about modern public health, show awareness of the shift in the nature of health problems across the twentieth century: from infectious diseases (tuberculosis, cholera) to non-communicable lifestyle diseases (heart disease, cancer, obesity). Examiners reward responses that show this transition rather than treating all health threats as the same type. For thematic essays, link modern campaigns (smoking ban, Change4Life) back to the same underlying driver as Victorian sanitation — government responding to evidence that preventable conditions are killing people — to show change and continuity together.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The 1919 Addison Act launched council house building to replace Victorian slums; slum clearance programmes in the 1930s removed the worst overcrowded housing, improving the health of thousands of working-class families.
  • The 1952 Great Smog led to the Clean Air Act 1956; research by Doll and Hill from 1950 led eventually to the 2007 smoking ban, reducing adult smoking rates from around 45 per cent to below 15 per cent over fifty years.
  • Twenty-first century public health shifted focus to obesity, diabetes and inactivity through campaigns like Change4Life and the sugar tax, while COVID-19 in 2020 demonstrated both the power and limits of modern public health infrastructure.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the government's response to the Great Smog of 1952.
practice_questions.marks: One feature with supporting detail. Example: The government passed the Clean Air Act 1956, which introduced smokeless zones banning the burning of coal in domestic fires in urban areas and setting emission standards for industry, to reduce the air pollution that had caused the Smog. [2 marks: 1 for feature, 1 for detail]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of government public health campaigns in the twenty-first century.
practice_questions.marks: Feature 1: The Change4Life campaign, launched in 2009, used advertising and community programmes to encourage healthier eating, more physical activity and reduced alcohol consumption, particularly targeting children and families. Feature 2: The sugar tax, introduced in 2018 on soft drinks, used taxation rather than persuasion to discourage consumption of high-sugar products linked to obesity and type 2 diabetes. [2 marks per feature]

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the introduction of the smoking ban in 2007 for public health in Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained explanation of one consequence (e.g. reduction in passive smoking in public places; decline in smoking rates over decades; reduced hospital admissions for smoking-related diseases; cultural normalisation of non-smoking) with embedded evidence. Secure: Clear consequence with evidence. Developing: Consequence identified, explanation limited. Emerging: Simple statement. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the council housing programme launched by the 1919 Addison Act for public health in Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Significance at the time (moved families from slums to homes with indoor sanitation and ventilation; reduced disease linked to overcrowding and damp) AND over time (established the principle that the state should provide housing for health reasons; continued by post-WWII slum clearance and tower block building). Secure: Both dimensions with evidence. Developing: One dimension. Emerging: Description only. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'Government campaigns have been more effective than legislation in improving public health in modern Britain.'
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Evaluates campaigns (Change4Life, five-a-day, NHS stop-smoking services — persuasion approach) against legislation (Clean Air Act 1956, smoking ban 2007, sugar tax 2018 — compulsion approach). Considers which has achieved more measurable impact. Substantiated conclusion. Secure: Both sides with evidence and conclusion. Developing: One side argued. Emerging: Descriptive. [12 marks]

practice_questions.text: How far has the focus of public health in Britain changed between 1900 and the present day? Use evidence to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Traces change (1900s housing/TB; 1950s air pollution/smoking; 1980s–2000s lifestyle diseases/obesity; 2020 COVID-19), weighs change against continuity (government always responding reactively to crises; quarantine and sanitation principles persist; health inequalities between rich and poor throughout). Substantiated judgement. Secure: Multiple periods with evidence. Developing: Two periods. Emerging: Single period. [16 marks]

flashcard_questions.a: Build council housing to meet local needs, with central government subsidies.

flashcard_questions.a: A toxic combination of fog and coal smoke that blanketed London in December 1952, killing thousands.

flashcard_questions.a: Smokeless zones banning coal burning in urban domestic fires, and emission standards for industry.

flashcard_questions.q: Who published research in 1950 linking smoking to lung cancer?
flashcard_questions.a: Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill.

flashcard_questions.a: A government initiative launched in 2009 to promote healthier eating, regular exercise and reduced alcohol consumption, especially for children.
A public health promotion encouraging people to eat five portions of fruit and vegetables daily.

flashcard_questions.a: Around 45 per cent in 1974; below 15 per cent by the 2020s.

flashcard_questions.a: Designated urban areas in which burning coal and smoky fuels was banned, requiring smokeless alternatives instead.
The planned demolition of overcrowded, dilapidated urban housing, generally replaced by new social housing.

glossary_terms.definition: Housing built and rented by local councils, intended to provide affordable, good-quality homes for working-class families.
The planned demolition of overcrowded, dilapidated urban housing, generally to be replaced by new social housing or open space.
Designated areas in which the burning of coal and other smoky fuels was banned or heavily restricted, requiring the use of smokeless fuels instead.
A government initiative launched in 2009 to encourage healthier lifestyles in England through exercise, diet and other health-promoting behaviours.
A nationwide restriction requiring people to stay at home except for essential reasons, used in Britain during the COVID-19 pandemic from March 2020.
